newsitem.title: USA: Weekly jobless claims down last week.
newsitem.headline: Weekly jobless claims down last week.

text.p: Fewer Americans waited on unemployment lines to collect benefits last week compared with the week before, the government said Thursday.
The Labour Department said jobless claims in the week ended March 1 dipped to 310,000, from 316,000 in the previous week. Wall Street economists had forecast initial jobless claims of 317,000.
A key gauge of jobless trends -- the department's four-week moving average -- continued its descent, falling to its lowest level in nearly eight years.
The average stood at 310,000 last week, down from 313,500 the previous week. It was at its lowest level since the week ended May 13, 1989, the department said.
It said seven states reported decreases in claims exceeding 1,000 on an unadjusted basis in the week ended Feb. 22, the latest period for which data are available.
They were New York, with 2,889 fewer new filings; Ohio, down 2,597; Pennsylvania, down 2,209; Arkansas, down 1,513; South Carolina, down 1,351; Maryland, down 1,153; and Michigan, down 1,133.
New York and Arkansas linked the drop to a shorter work week due to the President's Day holiday.
Pennsylvania reported fewer layoffs in the construction, trade, and lumber and wood industries, while South Carolina said it had fewer layoffs in the apparel industry.

Maryland reported fewer layoffs in the publishing, optical goods, trade, and service industries. Michigan had fewer layoffs in various industries throughout the state. Ohio gave no reason for its decline.

Six states reported increases in claims exceeding 1,000 in the Feb. 22 week. They were Massachusetts, with 3,545 additional new filings; North Carolina, with 2,345; California, with 1,645; Connecticut, 1,422, Rhode Island, with 1,152; and Texas, with 1,085.
Massachusetts had layoffs in the service industry, while North Carolina reported layoffs in the construction and textile industries.

Rhode Island attributed the increase in claims to layoffs in the trade and service industries and in manufacturing, while Texas said it had layoffs in the rubber and electrical equipment industries. California and Connecticut gave no explanation for their increases.
